text.p: Australian grain markets continued to fall during the past week under the weight of a very big crop, concern that the handling system will feel the strain, and the continued threat of rain during harvest.

Australian Wheat Board (AWB) indicator cash prices for Australian Standard White (ASW) fell by between A$7.00 and A$13.00 a tonne depending on delivery point, while futures prices generally fell by about A$6.00 over the week.
By Friday, brokers and traders were saying Australian prices could not fall much more before growers would refuse to sell.
Even so, if Chicago continued to fall the Australian market would not be able to hold up on its own, one trader said.

Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd chartists are tipping the January 1997 futures contract will fall to A$130.00 a tonne now that the A$150.00 a tonne support level is broken. This contract fell by a further A$5.50 to A$147.00 on Friday.

Tuesday's Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics forecast of a 20.9 million tonne 1996/97 wheat crop, up from the 17.0 million tonnes produced in 1995/96 and from the agency's previous forecast of 18.8 million tonnes for the latest year, added to downward pressure on wheat prices.
The AWB's A$5.00 a tonne pools prices cuts on Monday, bringing ASW back to A$190.00, was less than the market had expected but failed to slow the general decline.

Representatives of Geneva-based international wheat trader Romak were visiting the AWB on Friday looking to discuss the purchase of a significant tonnage, Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders, Romak's Australian arm, told Reuters.
Howard would bot say more. But a potential Romak buy was one of the few positive signals to emerge during the week.

The weather provided some encouragement with rain failing to cause a significant downgrading of harvest wheat in the past week. But the threat of a wet harvest will not be over until mid-November, when the harvest moves fully begins in New South Wales (NSW), which has overtaken Western Australia (WA) this year as Australia's biggest wheat state.
There was excellent weather in the New England area of NSW at present as harvesting began, Howard said. Weather damage so far was confined to southern Queensland, he said.
"For the most part things are pretty good in the central grain belt," he said.
Howard reported a very sharp decline in cash barley prices during the past week, by about A$14.00 a tonne to about A$117.00 a tonne delivered Whyalla. "That's pretty horrific," he said.
Cash wheat was not active enough to yield firm prices, but would have declined by at least A$15.00 over the week, he said.
Another trader described wheat as under strong stress.
With the pool price at A$190.00 and ASW wheat traded freely in Newcastle at A$150.00, there was general concensut the pool price could easily fall a further SA$10.00, he said.
After a further A$4.00 a tonne price cut on Friday, the AWB's indicative price for new crop ASW wheat Newcastle fell by a total of A$10.00 a tonne to A$138.00 over the week.

Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) market leader January 1997 fell by A$5.50 to A$147.00 while January 1998 also fell by A$5.50 to A$140.50 over the week. SFE volume rose on profit-taking to 167 lots against 89 the week before.
